The Detcore half of https://github.com/rrnewton/hermit/issues/4483 ("DBT: a fork from a non-leader thread kills the run").
- **Head:** 33e7329a823e7fb05b4071b3e6e7654888646769, one commit on main d9351f50.
- **Pairing:** lands with https://github.com/rrnewton/reverie/pull/1085 at 612a12a1653b16b5b75669661409894eb87d96ca, a fast-forward of reverie main 9547c359 that both reviewers approved.
- **Changes since the reviewed 7527eced:** the sliced, disposition-following wait; the fork-synch restart test; the mask assertion; trigger 4. The commit message has the full text.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

The owner asked on 2026-10-19 that every decision that changes what the guest sees be made in Detcore, not in the vendored DynamoRIO. Reverie now provides only the mechanism: an injected pselect6 sleeps under the mask the Tool passes, and an interruption by DynamoRIO's own signal is reported as ERESTARTNOHAND. A new capability, `restarts_backend_interrupted_waits` (DBT only), states that contract.

Before: under DBT, a select or pselect6 on more than 64 descriptors was injected raw. DynamoRIO's suspend signal, sent on every retry of a fork's synch, ended the wait with an EINTR that Linux never returns.

After: `detcore/src/syscalls/restartable_wait.rs` makes Linux's decisions inside one BlockingExternalIO grant.
- **Deadline:** set when the call enters, from the timeout as `kern_select` / `do_pselect` validate and normalize it.
- **Slices:** the wait runs as kernel waits of at most 50 ms. Each slice starts under a mask computed from the dispositions at that moment: the guest's mask plus the signals whose delivery would not end the wait (`KernelSignalState::interrupting`). So when another thread installs a handler during the wait and then sends the signal, the wait ends with EINTR, as on Linux. A slice that times out before the deadline restores the descriptor sets the kernel cleared.
- **ERESTARTNOHAND:** the kernel wait runs again toward the same deadline and only the timeout is rewritten. That path takes no lock: if the fork synch gives up on the waiter, the child inherits whatever the waiter holds.
- **STICKY_TIMEOUTS:** read per call.
- **Write-back:** as Linux does it: a truncated timeval, or a timespec, or nothing under STICKY_TIMEOUTS.

DBT's runtime always states the capability. The legacy DBT configuration form derives it the same way it derives `promotes_open_files_before_native_lifecycle`, so the guest-visible configuration bytes do not change. The routine asserts that the capability is never combined with `models_signal_targets`.

**Not matched:** a signal that arrives while it is ignored, and whose action changes before the wait ends, is delivered later under the new action. Linux discards it on arrival. Matching that needs DynamoRIO to drop guest-ignored signals on receipt. This is recorded in the module and in the follow-up issue.

**Still slow (step 2):** a fork takes about 51 s while another thread waits.

## Determinism

All kernel waits stay inside the one grant of an external wait that was already host-timed. No turn, virtual-time charge or INFO log is added per slice or per restart, and the thread rejoins the schedule once. Which signals end the wait depends on the guest's mask and on the dispositions when the signal arrives (to within one slice), never on when DynamoRIO's signal arrived. Every other backend reports the capability false and keeps its old path.

## Linux Semantics

Linux v7.1:
- [fs/select.c](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/fs/select.c?h=v7.1#n700) `kern_select` (700-731) sets the deadline at entry, and `do_pselect` (739-772) installs the mask.
- `core_sys_select` returns -ERESTARTNOHAND with the sets untouched (682); a timeout returns 0 with the sets cleared.
- [`poll_select_finish`](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/fs/select.c?h=v7.1#n295) (295-365) writes the time left back, except under STICKY_TIMEOUTS (306).
- [kernel/signal.c `sig_ignored`](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/kernel/signal.c?h=v7.1#n106) (106-124): an ignored, unblocked signal is discarded when sent, and `get_signal` uses the action current at delivery.
- [arch/x86/kernel/signal.c](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/arch/x86/kernel/signal.c?h=v7.1#n333): with no handler, -ERESTARTNOHAND restarts (347); with a handler, it becomes -EINTR (268).

Natively, DynamoRIO's signal does not exist, so running the wait again toward the same deadline reproduces the uninterrupted call. `tests/c/select_many_descriptors.c` (pipe at descriptor 100) checks these cases:
- data arrives;
- SIGCHLD at its default does not end the wait;
- a caught SIGUSR1 ends it with EINTR;
- **SIGUSR1 ignored at entry, then caught and sent by another thread with no data: EINTR, handler run once** (Codex's case);
- 0.3 s timeouts with write-back;
- tv_usec 1300000 and -1;
- STICKY_TIMEOUTS.

DBT and ptrace print the 16 lines that native prints.

## Validation

At 33e7329a, debug, devserver, load 30-80:
- **Build and static checks:** fmt, metadata --locked, build, check, `clippy -D warnings`, and the bare-URL check are clean. Pin uniformity OK; Buck inventory 992; footprint and DAG checks clean. `check-reverie-pin` blocks only until 612a12a1 is on reverie main.
- **Unit tests:** detcore lib 2143/2143, detcore-model 240/240, detcore-dbt 54/54, golden 2/2. manifest-plan 624/624 (8 threads).
- **Wide run:** every dbt/select test plus `external_signal_interrupt`, 317/317 at -j 48.
- **New fork-synch test:** `run_dbt_select_restarts_through_a_fork_synch_as_linux` lets a helper fork during the wait. `-synch_all_threads_max_loops 600`, passed through the new Hermit-side `HERMIT_DBT_TEST_DYNAMORIO_OPTIONS`, bounds the synch to about 3 s. Modes `fork` and `fork-sticky` (2 s STICKY_TIMEOUTS) must equal native, and the debug log must show the restarts (about 385-600). With the existing select test, run together 10/10, 9.3-10.2 s each.
- **Mutation arms**, each restored:
  - no restart: errno 514;
  - timeout never shrinks: sticky gives r=1;
  - write-back ignoring sticky: the timeout differs;
  - mask computed once: Codex's case gives r=0 and the handler never runs;
  - sets not restored: hangs.
  - Control passes.
- **L2:** `--strict --verify --verify-strict`, DBT and ptrace: matched, `bitwise_parity: true`, 404 and 520 INFO messages, default log, no relaxations.
- **38 runs of the 4483 fork programs under DBT:** identical to the previous head. The 32 runs without an external signal print native output; the 6 signal runs behave as on Linux.

## Human Review Required

Trigger 2: a Reverie `Backend` capability and the injected-wait contract. Trigger 4, as Codex argued: the call holds its grant across backend interruptions and runs as sliced kernel waits, which changes when the thread can rejoin. No scheduler.rs, run-queue, virtual-time or race-search code changes.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

`hermit run --chaos --replay-schedule-from=<record>` now makes the same scheduling decisions as the same replay without `--chaos`, and three causes of scheduler turns that a replay added to its record are fixed (below). With them fixed, the public test guest's chaos records (seeds 1-3, with and without its system calls) and five chaos records of a real crashing program replay to their recorded output, with and without `--chaos`. That is what was measured, not a claim that every record now replays faithfully: seed 7 of the system-call guest still diverges, for a different reason (see Not claimed). `hermit analyze` passes `--chaos` to every trial, including the two replays that verify its endpoints, so before this it could stop on a real crashing program with `Error: the passing schedule endpoint did not reproduce a passing outcome` (exit 125) before its first bisection step.

The replayed schedule decides where each slice ends and which thread runs next. Three things added scheduler turns the record does not have. Each committed turn advances the virtual clock by 0.5 ms, so the guest read another time and could take another path:

- **Chaos still drew under a schedule replay** (commit 1). A schedule replay with `--chaos` drew an exponential slice end for every slice, a random priority at every slice end, and yield epochs for `sched_yield`. A drawn slice end ended the slice early. `Config::chaos_draws_schedule()` (`--chaos`, unless a schedule is replayed) now gates those three decisions. A replay with `--chaos` makes exactly the decisions a replay without it makes, and once its schedule runs out it goes on as a run without `--chaos`, as that replay does. `--chaos-per-thread-slowdown` changes virtual time rather than scheduling and stays on. A replay can reproduce it only when given the recorded run's scheduler seed and slowdown options. Whether it then does is not measured, and doubtful: a slice end replayed as an administrative checkpoint turn does not pass through `next_timeslice`, which installs slowdown epochs.
- **A timer preemption ended its slice twice** (commit 2). Chaos records carry callback checkpoints for slices that end in software (#4582). When the record ended a timer-preempted slice in the timer's post-hook within one RCB of the PMU maximum (`PosthookPmuEpsilon`), the replay reached the recorded branch count already in the pre-hook and ended the slice there. The checkpoint then ended the next slice in the post-hook. The pre-hook now leaves the end to the checkpoint when the next checkpoint is in the running callback at the same progress at a later site.
- **A checkpoint turn kept a stale backstop** (commit 2). A checkpoint the replay applies as an administrative turn keeps the slice. It also kept the slice's `--max-timeslice` backstop, counted from the slice's old start, which then ended the next slice where the record has no end. The administrative turn now restarts the backstop from the checkpoint, as the recorded run's new slice did, while the backstop is still the slice end (`ThreadState::replay_backstop`). Any other slice end stays: a deadline the replayed schedule set, or one an exec resumed. Commit 3 makes that hold even when such a deadline falls on the backstop's very nanosecond (see Revision 3).

The second and third also break replays without `--chaos` on current main. Of 5 chaos recordings of a real crashing program, main replayed 4 to a SIGSEGV instead of the recorded exit 0, with `--chaos` and without it, and none to the recorded syscall log. With this branch all 5 replay both ways with identical syscall logs, every virtual time included. `hermit analyze` on that program then verifies its endpoints and finishes; that run also needs our open analyze pull requests (see Validation).

## Determinism

- `chaos_draws_schedule()` reads only the configuration. It covers what `--chaos` draws; what `--fuzz-seed` draws (targeted chaos, `--chaos-target-races`, and `--fuzz-futexes`) the scheduler gates on those flags, not on `--chaos`, so adding `--chaos` to a schedule replay changes none of it, and a replay draws it again from its own `--fuzz-seed`, so it reproduces it only when given the recorded run's (revision 12). Under a schedule replay a slice now ends at the replayed schedule's deadline or at the backstop, which `next_timeslice` already installed for a replay without `--chaos`. Nothing is drawn from the thread's chaos generator (`chaos_schedule_replay_draws_no_slice_end` checks the generator is untouched). For every other run, `chaos_draws_schedule()` equals `chaos`: ordinary chaos runs, recording, and preemption replay (`--replay-preemptions-from`, whose chaos path consumes recorded points) are unchanged.
- The pre-hook deferral reads the next recorded checkpoint and the running callback's progress, both functions of the record and of the events observed so far. The callback does not run guest code between its pre-hook and its post-hook, so the slice ends at the same virtual time and RCB count either way. The deferral removes only the second end.
- The backstop restart sets the slice end to `now + --max-timeslice` in the thread's own virtual time. This is the value `next_timeslice` sets at every new slice of a schedule replay. `replay_backstop` is set only by `next_timeslice` and by the restart. Every writer of a slice end the schedule decides clears it (`ThreadState::install_schedule_deadline`: the replayer's deadline, an exec's resumed deadline, the no-RCB-time fallback). The restart also acts only while `end_of_timeslice` still equals it, as a guard against writers not named here. Which slice end is the backstop is therefore decided by where it came from, not by its value (commit 3). It is serialized with `#[serde(default)]` and starts `None` in a new thread.
- No change coarsens, freezes or resets virtual time. Each removes a scheduler turn the record does not have, so the replay's clock follows the recorded one. The guest's printed virtual times match the recording to the nanosecond in the runs below.
- Recorded schedules, `RECORD_VERSION` and recording itself are unchanged. The strict slice-boundary replay (`--strict-schedule-boundaries`) refuses `--chaos` and has its own cursor. It is unchanged.

## Linux Semantics

No syscall result, errno, signal or `/proc` content changes. A replayed program now sees the virtual times of the run it replays rather than later ones, so a replay makes the syscalls the recording made.

## Design

1. **The mark.** `SchedEvent` gains `stopless: bool`, with `#[serde(default)]`.
   - `update_logical_time_rcbs` marks the `Branch` event of an end that `catch_up_lone_slice_ends` processes (`SchedEvent::taken_without_stop`). It reads no registers for that event: the guest stopped later, so the event has no `end_rip`.
   - Per-thread preemption rows, chaos epochs and callback checkpoints come from the end's branch count and event progress, so they are written as a stop writes them.
2. **Serialization.** `Serialize` is written by hand.
   - Human-readable formats leave the field out when it is false, so a record without such ends is byte for byte what it was.
   - Binary formats always write it. `SchedEvent` crosses Reverie's GlobalRPC, which is positional bincode; the ptrace backend round-trips every request through it in debug builds. Binary `SchedEvent`s are never persisted.
   - `Debug` also omits the field when false, so INFO logs of runs without such ends are unchanged.
3. **Replayer.** `Replayer::resolve_time_to_run` returns a `ReplayedSliceEnd` (length, stopless).
   - A stopless `Branch` always ends a slice. The thread's own check-in can follow it with no branch in between, and the existing patterns read that shape as branches that reach a check-in, with no slice end. Two of the 7,539 stopless ends of the aarch64 recording above have that shape.
   - The flag reaches the thread through `ReplayAction`, `ConsumeResult` and `TraceSchedEventResponse`. It travels only in a `Continue` after the observed event matched, so only to the thread whose own next event the end is. A context switch, or an unmatched event, hands the end on with a stop.
   - Every `TraceSchedEventResponse` sets `ThreadState::replayed_stopless_end` anew: the end's branch count, or none. The length is the recorded count (`LogicalTime::from_rcbs`), which `into_rcbs` gives back exactly. Where the clock runs at another rate the armed end differs from this count, so the end keeps its stop.
   - A thread that a replayed context switch resumes gets only a length through its grant (the `timeslices` map), so it takes its first end with a stop.
4. **Detcore.** `Detcore::replay_allows_stopless_end` gates both `skips_lone_slice_end` and the end of `catch_up_lone_slice_ends`.
   - In a schedule replay it allows only the recorded stopless end.
   - In a preemption replay it allows the recorded end (`ThreadState::replay_rcb_end`), or the thread's maximum once the record is used up.
   - A record with per-thread chaos rates installs a recorded rate at slice ends whatever the run's flags say. Its ends keep their stops, as `--chaos-per-thread-slowdown` keeps them in a run that records.
5. **Matching.** `is_hard_desync` and `hard_desync_fields` accept a stop observed where the record has a stopless end, never the reverse. `split-branches` and analyze's fragments keep the mark only on the fragment that ends where the original did.
6. **Analyze.** Analyze compares runs that differ in where their threads ran alone, so its comparisons ignore how an end was taken.
   - `SchedEvent::same_kind` and `same_operations` compare two events either way. Needleman-Wunsch scoring, the common prefix and postfix, `same_event_except_count`, `test_exact_replay` and bisect's identical-trace check use them.
   - Those two are not transitive, so they cannot key a hash. The event permutation (`generate_permutation`) therefore aligns on `alignment_keys`, where a Branch event stands for its thread's branch total at its end instead of its end RIP. The total also keeps apart equal-sized batches that the RIP used to separate.
7. **Gating.** `Config::replays_lone_preemptions` no longer excludes recorded or replayed preemptions and schedules. Strict schedule boundaries stay excluded, as do the other conditions #4662 lists. As in #4662, any reply that is not a lone grant clears the mark, a `TraceSchedEvent` reply included. A recording therefore keeps a stop at the first end after each check-in: 2 of 7,541 ends on the aarch64 case, 12 of 3,757 on a loop guest.

## Record format and versions

Only the preemption record (`--record-preemptions-to`, read by `--replay-schedule-from`, `--replay-preemptions-from`, analyze and bisect) changes. `hermit record` recordings do not hold one, so `RECORD_VERSION` is unchanged.
- **Older records** have no field. They read as records whose ends all had stops and replay exactly as before; no replay takes one of their ends without a stop.
- **Older Hermit reading a new record** refuses it. A record that holds the mark is preemption format 5 (`STOPLESS_SLICE_ENDS_FORMAT`, the next above main's format 4 for background starts): a Hermit that reads formats 1 to 4 refuses format 5 as a format it does not know, before the guest starts, and a mark in a record of an older format is refused by name. Only a writer that notes its run's background starts (a recording, a preemption replay's re-record) writes the mark; a record that keeps no starts states format 3 on main (a schedule replay's re-record, a shorter prefix, an edit, an analyze or bisect trial) and keeps no marks either, so its replay stops at those ends, which replays the run as faithfully. A mark on an event with an end RIP, or on one that is not a Branch, is refused wherever a record is built, written or read. Records without the mark keep their format. The user guide says so.

## Determinism

#4662 shows a slice end whose grant found the thread alone can be processed at the thread's next entry into Detcore. The requests, passes and state come out the same, because two things hold:
- nothing but the thread's own requests can act before that entry;
- the end reads nothing from the guest but its branch count.

A recording read one more thing at an end: the instruction pointer for its event. A stopless end records none, and the rest of the record follows from the count. A replay takes an end without a stop only when its own grant is lone, by the same predicate, so the argument holds for the replayed run too. A schedule replay also takes only ends its recording took that way, so every instruction pointer the recording read is still checked.

Virtual time stays continuous and is not coarsened: every retired branch and turn charge is applied as before. The validation compares committed global time at every recorded event, not a final total.

## Linux Semantics

No guest-visible behavior changes. The guest never observes a slice end, and none of the changed code reads or writes guest state.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

`hermit analyze --minimize` checks its failing endpoint with a schedule replay. A preemption replay ends slices only where its record says, so its slices can run far past `--max-timeslice`; the schedule replay instead ended every slice at that bound, left the record (RCB-TIME-DESYNC), and could take the passing path, so minimize reported the endpoint did not reproduce the failure even when it had.

A record now carries `uncapped_slices` (the latest virtual event time) when its slices ran without the bound. A schedule replay of a marked record ends slices where the record does while the record lasts, then returns to the bound. Unmarked records replay exactly as before.

## Determinism

The mark and the backstop (mark plus `--max-timeslice`) are pure functions of the recorded virtual event times and configuration, never host time. Every replay of the same record under the same options takes the same slice ends; after the record runs out, slices are bounded again.

## Linux Semantics

No guest-visible behaviour changes. Only where a schedule replay of a marked record ends its slices changes, to match the recorded run.

## Determinism

Only tests change, apart from the `scan_after` extraction, which keeps the same decision for every input. So no run's schedule, events or results change.

The end-to-end test checks counts that are a function of the files' bytes: pairs, rewritten, left and failed. The guest's counter is exact by construction, under any schedule. The store-exclusive check needs only zero failures, plus zero executions where the counters ran for the whole run. Neither depends on host timing once every loop is rewritten.

## Linux Semantics

No intercepted syscall's behaviour changes. The tests rely on the same kernel behaviour as #4795, and the citations there apply:

- A forced `/proc/<pid>/mem` write to a private read-only mapping copies the page for that process (`mem_rw()` sets `FOLL_FORCE | FOLL_WRITE`, [fs/proc/base.c:857](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/fs/proc/base.c?h=v6.1#n857); `check_vma_flags()` allows it only on a COW mapping, [mm/gup.c:1064-1078](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/mm/gup.c?h=v6.1#n1064)). That is why the file and the second mapping keep the loop.
- `/proc/<pid>/map_files` opens only with `CAP_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE` or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` ([fs/proc/base.c:2245-2249](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/fs/proc/base.c?h=v6.1#n2245)), which is why the rename test branches on it.
- `munmap` and `mprotect` act on whole pages, and the length is rounded up (`PAGE_ALIGN(len)`), which is what `page_span` models and the tests assert.

On Linux 6.12 and later, `proc_mem.force_override=never` (or `=ptrace`, or a build-time default to either) refuses the forced write. The runtime tests that write probe for it first and skip with a message.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

The aarch64 exclusive-loop rewriter now covers two loop shapes that Rust's standard library compiles into Android's linker and every Rust-linked library, and that it used to leave alone. A loop the rewrite leaves alone can fail its store-exclusive a different number of times from run to run. Each failure adds retired branches that a recorded preemption may not replay. These loops sit on the panic, thread-teardown and contended-lock paths.

| Shape | Rust source | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A read-modify-write whose ALU instruction sets the flags, read by a branch after the loop | `Arc::drop` (`fetch_sub` then `== 1`) | `undecoded-instruction` | `rmw`: `LDADD` of the negated operand, then the original `SUBS` on the returned value |
| A compare-and-swap whose retry branches to a block before the loop that recomputes the new value | `compare_exchange_weak` in `fetch_update` (`ThreadId::new`) | `no-paired-load` | `cas-compare`, with the replacement it already had |

What is left, and why:
- **New value computed after the compare** (4 loops).
  - The shape is `LDxXR Rt; CMP Rt, Re; B.NE out; ADD Rv, ...; STxXR Ws, Rv; CBNZ`.
  - A CAS needs the new value in a register before it runs. On its mismatch path, the original changes only Rt and the flags, and both are still needed there. With six instructions to replace, there is no room to restore a third register.
  - A rewrite needs a seventh instruction, or proof that the failure path overwrites the register before reading it. In `read_contended` it does, but in `rust_panic_with_hook` the register is `x8` before a call, where AAPCS64 lets the callee read it.
- **Rotated compare-and-swaps** (`futex_rwlock::wake_writer_or_readers`, and against zero in `futex_mutex::lock_contended`), which store first and are entered at their load.
  - A six-instruction replacement exists for the wake path, but it must give up the loop's `CLREX`, which the same function's first attempt joins with a `B.NE`.
  - Skipping a `CLREX` on that path is observable. A later store-exclusive the rewrite leaves alone can then succeed where the original's must fail. The Codex seat's review showed this under QEMU: status 1 and memory 7 before, status 0 and memory 9 after.
  - This PR therefore does not rewrite them.

What changes:
- `detcore/src/aarch64_lse/insn.rs`: `ADDS`/`SUBS` decode as `Alu { sets_flags: true }`; `CMN` and a discarding form still decode as `Other`.
- `detcore/src/aarch64_lse/rewrite.rs`:
  - The store's `CBNZ` may retry anywhere outside the sequence. The sequence then starts at the nearest load-exclusive within three instructions, and a retry into the sequence after its first instruction is refused.
  - `rmw` admits a flag-setting `ADDS`/`SUBS`.
  - The new refusal `NewValueAfterCompare`.
- `detcore/src/aarch64_lse/elf.rs`: the report name `new-value-after-compare`.

## Determinism

The rewrite replaces a loop whose store-exclusive can fail spuriously with a single FEAT_LSE atomic that cannot. Each replacement ends in exactly the states the original loop can end in, but it takes a number of retired branches that does not depend on monitor timing.

- **Flag-setting read-modify-write.**
  - The original: `LDxXR Rt; SUBS Rv, Rt, #k; STxXR Ws, Rv; CBNZ Ws`.
  - The replacement: `MOVN Ws, #(k-1); LDADD{A}{L} Ws, Rt, [Xn]; SUBS Rv, Rt, #k; MOV Ws, wzr`.
  - The `SUBS` runs on the value the atomic replaced, which is the value the original's successful store-exclusive replaced. Nothing after it in either sequence sets the flags, so the flags at the exit are the original's, and so are Rt, Rv and Ws (0).
  - Only unshifted-register and 12-bit-immediate `ADDS`/`SUBS` with a real destination gain `sets_flags`, and only `rmw` reads it.
- **Compare-and-swap retrying elsewhere.** The retry runs only when the store-exclusive fails. A CAS never fails, so every execution of the replacement corresponds to one where the original's first store-exclusive succeeded. The rewriter refuses a retry into the sequence after its first instruction (the replacement would then be entered part-way). The existing check, that no branch from elsewhere enters the sequence part-way, still applies.
- **Orderings.** The acquire comes from the load and the release from the store, as for every other idiom.

## Linux Semantics

No system call, signal or `/proc` behaviour changes. The behaviour matched is the A64 architecture's: the load/store-exclusive pair and its monitors (the Arm ARM's "Synchronization and semaphores"), and `CAS`, `LDADD` and `SUBS` (Arm ARM DDI 0487 L.a, C6.2). The replacement words are llvm-mc's encodings, which the unit tests compare against.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

ps and pgrep read every process's `/proc/<pid>/status`. On KVM that failed
for every process but the reader (EACCES live, ENOENT for a zombie: whatever
host task held the number), and the reader's own status was the provider's
13 lines. On ptrace another process's status was the host's, sanitized, with
a zombie as `S (sleeping)`. Detcore, the one shared determinism engine, now
renders a task's `status` in Linux 6.17's line order, each line from the
source that answers the guest's own matching query in the same run: another
task's on ptrace and KVM, the reader's own on KVM (package K item 2b, slice
2b-2). After: the status guest equals native line for line at L2 on both.

Full detail: the commit messages of e1155e51 (the slice) and
0c38cc5fc9534ab8af2c890116a8fc1d56d8044c (the fix below).

## Background

Stacked on https://github.com/rrnewton/hermit/pull/5139 (2b-1). Design:
dev-hermit `ai_docs/2026-11-03-kvm-other-process-proc-design.md` section 6
item 2, and the coordinator's 2b-2 line rule (a line is rendered only from
the source that answers its syscall; no container constants).

## Expectation changes

- KVM, another task: EACCES/ENOENT -> rendered.
- KVM, own status: 13 provider lines -> rendered. Gains Vm* (0 kB), Groups,
  NS*, Kthread, Sig*, Cap*, Cpus/Mems, ctxt lines; State `R (running)` as
  Linux. Loses Umask and FDSize (no repeatable source; omitted list).
- ptrace, another task: zombie `Z (zombie)` (was `S`); Vm* padded to 8
  columns as `task_mem` prints; omitted lines and CapBnd/CapAmb gone (they
  showed the host container's values).
- ptrace own status, DBT, SaBRe, LiteInst: unchanged.
- system-utils/ps-proc-table stays disabled on KVM; reason now names cmdline
  (2b-3) and /proc/1/stat.

## Determinism

Name, State, ids, NS*, Threads and affinity come from the process-table
facts 2b-1's stat uses (no wire change; revision 39, digest unchanged).
Uid/Gid are Detcore's virtual root; Groups the reader's injected
`getgroups` (`setgroups` is a no-op); Sig* the backend's `signal_sets` of
the stopped thread with its published guest mask; CapInh/Prm/Eff an
injected `capget` of the task; CapBnd/CapAmb the reader's own prctl
answers, for its own thread only. A line whose source does not answer is
left out the same way every run. Lines with no source for any task are one
list, `procfs::task_status::OMITTED_STATUS_LINES`: Umask, FDSize,
CoreDumping, THP_enabled, untag_mask, SigQ, NoNewPrivs, Seccomp,
Seccomp_filters, Speculation_Store_Bypass, SpeculationIndirectBranch. Which
statuses are rendered is decided by declared capabilities, not backend
names.

Per-syscall sources (measured, both backends): Detcore answers getuid
family, sched_getaffinity, get_mempolicy, getrusage, getrlimit, getpgid/
getsid, ARCH_GET_UNTAG_MASK (EINVAL), PR_GET_NO_NEW_PRIVS/SECCOMP/
SPECULATION_CTRL (ENOSYS). Passed through (host kernel / KVM executor):
getgroups, capget, umask, PR_CAPBSET_READ, PR_CAP_AMBIENT,
PR_GET_THP_DISABLE. All agree across backends except `capget` of another
process (KVM: ESRCH).

Parity residuals: P1 ptrace's own status stays the kernel's (KVM's is
rendered); P2 another task's CapInh/Prm/Eff present on ptrace, absent on
KVM, following `capget`; P3 SigIgn shows each backend's inherited
dispositions (ptrace adds SIGTTIN, SIGTTOU, signal 32).

Fidelity residuals: Linux prints these lines on every kernel we emulate, so each is a named residual with a P1 task:
- NoNewPrivs, Seccomp, Seccomp_filters (Detcore answers the prctls with ENOSYS): minibeads dh-01wr0.
- Another task's CapBnd/CapAmb, and Cap* of another process on KVM (P2): dh-25gcx.
- FDSize and Umask: dh-09ffe.
- SigQ, CoreDumping, THP_enabled, untag_mask: dh-m62rg.
- A zombie's SigPnd, ShdPnd, SigBlk, SigIgn and SigCgt (no backend reports an exited thread's signal sets; found by musereviewc): dh-yx74r.
- Speculation_* lines are omitted as kernel- and CPU-dependent.
- A zombie's Sig* lines are absent, because no backend reports an exited thread's sets.

## Linux Semantics (linux-6.17)

- `fs/proc/array.c` `proc_pid_status` (:439-465): no permission check;
  memory, CoreDumping, THP_enabled, untag_mask only with an mm (:449-455),
  so a zombie has none.
- `proc_task_name` (:99-118): Name escapes only `\n` and `\\` (:115).
- `task_state` (:148-225): Umask only with fs (:179-180); State from
  `task_state_array` (:126-140); Groups space-joined plus a trailing space
  (:199-206); NS* per level (:209-220); Kthread (:224).
- `fs/proc/task_mmu.c` `task_mem`: values right-aligned in 8 columns.
- `task_sig` (:264-301), `task_cap` (:311-331).

## Relationship to gVisor

gVisor's sentry renders `/proc/[pid]/status` from its own task and
credential model (`pkg/sentry/fsimpl/proc`), never the host. Same position
here: Detcore owns the model and renders; the backend only intercepts.
Where Detcore has no source for a line it omits and names it rather than
copying a host or container value.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

ps, pgrep and pkill read every process's `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, and tools
read `environ`. On KVM, reading another process's `cmdline` was refused by
name (the run stopped with exit 122). Every `environ`, the reader's own
included, gave the KVM provider's EACCES. Detcore, the one shared
determinism engine, now serves both on KVM (package K item 2b, slice 2b-3):
- another process's from the strings its image's `execve` passed;
- the reader's own `environ` from its memory;
- with Linux's access check at the open, and Linux's pinning of `environ`
  to the image its open found.

After: the guest equals native line for line at L2 on ptrace and KVM, and
pgrep/pkill match on KVM.

Full detail: the commit messages of 6770ab498fc17b9454d63fac7d0f7d54078eec65 and its parent.

## Background

Stacked on #5144 (2b-2), which is on #5139 (2b-1). Design: dev-hermit
`ai_docs/2026-11-03-kvm-other-process-proc-design.md` section 6 item 3, and
the coordinator's 2b-3 rulings (a record-based fallback keyed on the
capability; ptrace keeps the kernel's file).

## One semantics, and the interim fallback

Linux shows the target's areas as they are in its memory at each read,
`setproctitle` included. Reading that memory is the target on every
backend: ptrace gets it from the kernel's file, and the caller's own files
read its own memory. Where `tool_can_name_guest_descriptors` is false
(KVM), the tool cannot read another guest process's memory. Another
process's files therefore come from a record of its `execve` strings. This
is the named interim fallback, a backend-contract gap, not a per-backend
policy.

KNOWN LIMIT: a rewrite in memory after the exec is not shown to other
readers on KVM (P1 minibeads dh-ngy9z). The first read of a run served from
the record logs a WARN naming dh-ngy9z.

## Changes

- `ExecStrings { argv, envp }`, recorded in the image's first stop, only
  where the capability is false. Each record gets a run-unique image
  number. A fork inherits the record, an exec replaces it, an exit drops
  it.
- RPC: `RecordExecStrings` and `ProcessExecStrings` (whose response
  carries the image number), appended last. Revision 42, after 2b-1's 41,
  row `(42, "05097a2f4152ff09", ...)`. Digest domain 7 covers
  `ExecStrings`; the reserved list is unchanged. The advisory table numbers
  39 and 44 are released.
- New per-process kind `environ` (index 14, inode tag 0). It is mode 0400,
  and its open asks `auxv`'s check (`ptrace_read_allowed_for`, Linux
  `__mem_open`) and pins the process's current image number.
- KVM:
  - another process's `cmdline`/`environ` are rendered from the record (a
    process that has exited reads nothing);
  - the own `environ` reads own memory by Linux's `environ_read` rule;
  - an `environ` whose pinned image is no longer current reads 0;
  - directory listings show `cmdline` and `environ`.
- ptrace, DBT, SaBRe, LiteInst: unchanged (`kernel_serves_every_environ`).

## Determinism

The record is copied before the image runs, from bytes the loader wrote.
Every read is a pure function of the record, the read's position and count,
and the pinned/current image numbers. The global tool assigns those numbers
in the order of the serialized `RecordExecStrings` requests, and they never
reach the guest. The access answer is the existing auxv decision. No host
time, host `/proc` or backend name is read. The WARN is host-side:
`--verify` compares INFO records only (`is_info_detlog`).

## Linux Semantics (linux-6.17)

- fs/proc/base.c `get_mm_cmdline`: no open, `get_task_mm` at each read,
  so a kept `cmdline` follows an exec.
- `environ_open` = `__mem_open(PTRACE_MODE_READ)` pins the mm. `environ_read`
  returns 0 without an mm or when `mmget_not_zero` fails (a map an exec
  replaced), with page-sized reads and EFAULT on a short copy.
- Zombie: `cmdline` reads empty; `environ` is global root's 0400, so EACCES.
- fs/exec.c (since 5.18): an empty argv gets an empty `argv[0]`.

## Plain Language Summary and Project Impact

On Linux, `rt_sigsuspend` installs a temporary mask and sleeps until a signal that mask lets in arrives. A masked `ppoll` waits the same way. On KVM, neither did:
- KVM's own `rt_sigsuspend` never sleeps, so the guest got ENOSYS. In ledger row C a timer loop got 1 delivery of 20; a sibling's `tgkill` could not end the wait (#5040).
- A masked `ppoll` that would wait was refused (row F').

This is SIGSHARE S2b, stacked on S2a (#5166). On KVM, `rt_sigsuspend` now parks in the scheduler between two runs of the backend's own call. At the end of the step-2 drain, the scheduler wakes the waiter when backend-reported state shows a signal its temporary mask lets in. A masked `ppoll` polls with the backend's own probe. No reverie-kvm syscall code; ptrace, LiteInst, SaBRe, DBT unchanged.

**Scope:** sibling signals and Detcore-published timer signals. A child-exit SIGCHLD wait keeps today's ENOSYS until S4 (dh-ro7dr).

## Change (6 commits)

1. `scheduler/backend_signal_waits.rs` adds a scan that runs last in `step2_drain_prefix`, after every barrier.
   - It visits parked waiters in DetTid order.
   - It wakes a waiter for pending `& !held & !mask` signals that are caught, default-acting, or ignored (so the waiter can discard it).
   - It skips killed threads and any process holding an observed parked wait's permit.
2. `handle_rt_sigsuspend` (KVM) runs the backend's call. On ENOSYS it settles in the thread's own turn, then parks (`SleepUntil(INDEFINITE)`, `RT_SIGSUSPEND_FYI`).
3. `backend_masked_ppoll_wait` replaces the row F' refusal. Its own probes end the wait.
4. Tests and pins.
5-6. The review fixes F1 and F2 (below).

## Review round 1 (revastra2, CHANGES_REQUESTED at c1c6342f)

- **F1: mixed pending set.** c1c6342f removed every ignored let-in signal at once.
  - `settle_suspend_decline` walks Linux's dequeue order (`next_signal`/`dequeue_signal`) and discards only the ignored signals before the first delivered one, as `get_signal` does.
  - A stop first, or an ignored or stopping signal behind a delivered one, is refused by name before anything is removed: Linux's outcome depends on the handler's `sa_mask`, which `SignalSets` lacks (the masked-ppoll policy). F1 is closed as this support cut.
- **F2: an ignored signal sent during the wait.** Linux discards it at send, because `sig_ignored`/`prepare_signal` see it let in by the mask that sigsuspend installed. The backend kept it pending under the thread's own mask.
  - The scan now wakes the waiter so it discards the signal in its own turn.
  - An `rt_sigaction` that stops ignoring a signal first asks the scheduler (new RPC `SuspendHoldsDiscarded`, revision 50) whether a waiter still holds it, and yields while one does.
  - Not a general fix for S3 (LinuxEmu's ignored-generation residual).

## Review round 2 (revastra2 delta at 048870af: F1 closed, F2 open)

- **The gap:** the guard no longer saw a waiter the drain had woken (its request was the signal set, not the park) while the ignored signal was pending. Under `--chaos --chaos-target-races` the setter's yield was granted first, so the stale handler ran (revastra2's `root-sender` witness).
- **Fix:**
  - `backend_suspend_woken` keeps a woken suspend's temporary mask from any request replacement until the waiter's grant. In that turn the waiter removes the signal before it files anything else.
  - The guard counts parked and woken waiters alike, so the setter never proceeds while the obligation exists. After 1024 turns it refuses by name.
  - After the park, every ignored let-in signal arrived during the wait and was discarded at send, so all are removed in any order (no false mixed-set refusal).

## Determinism

1. The scan runs at one call site, under the maintenance guard (no turn held, no fence, reservation or registration outstanding).
2. At that point LinuxEmu's sets change only through committed events. The only exception is a delivery under an observed wait's permit, and the scan skips that process. An ordinary boundary permit dequeues inside its holder's own grant (the `select_parked_alarm` rule).
3. Every decision is a function of the committed prefix: DetTid order, the stable state, the request's mask, and the process tree. The settle step and the rt_sigaction guard read that state in the caller's turn; every yield is a scheduled turn.
4. No wake is lost. The call and the park happen in one turn, and the scan is level-triggered. A spurious wake re-runs the call and parks again.
5. Virtual time is never rounded. step2d reports a wait no signal can end as a deadlock.

A pre-code scheduling review's H1-H3, M4-M6, L8, L9 were adopted; a second found the narrowed H1 sound.

## Linux Semantics

- A wait ends when a pending signal unblocked by the temporary mask is caught or default-acting (`signal_pending` after `set_current_blocked`).
- Ignored signals follow `dequeue_signal` order and the discard at send.
- KVM returns EINTR with the temporary mask installed and the old mask saved.
- Refused by name: a stop, the mixed set, and the S4 SIGCHLD case (which keeps ENOSYS).
- **Known deviation (dh-02sy1):** between masked-ppoll probes the thread is under its own mask: a mid-wait `/proc` SigBlk read differs, and an ignored signal only ppoll's mask blocks is dropped early. Results, EINTR and delivery match Linux. Fix rides #5221.

## Relationship to gVisor

gVisor's `RtSigsuspend` sets the mask (`SetSignalMask`/`SetSavedSignalMask`), blocks in `t.Block`, returns ERESTARTNOHAND. Same split: LinuxEmu owns state and return; Detcore decides the wake.
